S6.excerpt:
`Retry-After` is the standard one. RFC 9110 allows either a number of seconds or an HTTP date, and a well-behaved client waits that long before retrying.
 Rate limit headers such as `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset`, or the older `X-RateLimit-` variants, expose the budget and when it resets. These are conventions, not part of RFC 9110, so check the API documentation for the exact names. [...] A 429 Too Many Requests means you hit a rate limit: the server is healthy and is deliberately refusing extra requests from this client for a while. It is a throttle, not an outage, and the response usually tells you exactly how long to wait.

## What a 429 means and what comes with it [...] The code itself. A rate limit answers 429. An overloaded or maintenance-mode server answers 503. Both may carry `Retry-After`, which is why people mix them up, but they mean different things: 429 says "you specifically are sending too much", 503 says "the service as a whole cannot take work right now". See the 503 guide for that side.

S8.title: 429 Too Many Requests - HTTP | MDN
S8.excerpt:
The HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` client error response status code indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. This mechanism of asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called "rate limiting".

A `Retry-After` header may be included to this response to indicate how long a client should wait before making the request again. [...] http

```
GET /reports/mdn HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com 
```

In this example, server-wide rate limiting is active when a client exceeds a set threshold of requests per minute. A 429 response is returned with a `Retry-After` header that indicates requests will be allowed for this client again after 3600 seconds (60 minutes):

http

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Content-Type: text/html Retry-After: 3600   Too Many Requests

# Too Many Requests

You're doing that too often! Try again later. [...] Implementations of rate limiting vary; restrictions may be server-wide or per resource. Typically, rate-limiting restrictions are based on a client's IP but can be specific to users or authorized applications if requests are authenticated or contain a cookie.

## Status

http

```
429 Too Many Requests 

## What RFC 429 (“Too Many Requests”) semantics/meaning are
The retrieved sources agree that **HTTP 429 indicates the client sent too many requests in a given amount of time**, i.e., **rate limiting / throttling** (the server is refusing additional requests from that client temporarily). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429] [https://www.host-tracker.com/en/learn/http-status-codes/429-too-many-requests] [https://community.auth0.com/t/too-many-requests-the-429-status-code-indicates-that-the-user-has-sent-too-many-requests-in-a-given-amount-of-time-rate-limiting-the-response-representations-should-include-details-explaining-the-condition-and-may-include-a-retry-after/203510]

bundles.question: According to the relevant RFC(s) for HTTP status code 429 “Too Many Requests,” which specific HTTP response header (exact header name) indicates how long a client should wait before retrying, and what exact meaning/semantics does the RFC assign to that header (including any explicit relationship to retry delay guidance such as Rate Limit or retry-after semantics)?
bundles.summary:
- **Which header name indicates the retry wait time?** The RFC defines that 429 responses **may** include the **`Retry-After`** header to indicate **how long to wait before making a new request**. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html]
- **HTTP 429 semantics and relationship to retry timing:** For **status code 429**, the RFC states the status indicates the user has sent **too many requests in a given amount of time (“rate limiting”)**. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html]
- **RFC guidance level/semantics for `Retry-After`:** In the 429 section, the response **“MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request.”** This explicitly ties `Retry-After` to the client’s retry/backoff timing for the rate-limited condition. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html]
- **Support/consistency with secondary sources:** MDN similarly summarizes that for 429, **`Retry-After` may be included** to indicate **how long a client should wait before making the request again**. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429]

**Answer (RFC-based):** The exact header name is **`Retry-After`**, and RFC 6585 assigns it the meaning of telling the client **the wait duration before retrying** in the **rate-limited (HTTP 429) condition**. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc6585.html]
